keyTakeaways: Prepare English surtitles from the current script, then review and rehearse them as performance text.
Translated surtitles and accessibility captions overlap, but captions may also need speakers, sound effects, music, and off-stage sound.
Choose projection, mobile viewing, or both according to the venue, audience, sightlines, language needs, and fallback plan.
A QR code is only an entry point; front-of-house guidance, network testing, operator rehearsal, and recovery planning complete the workflow.

faq.question: How do you add English surtitles to a non-English Fringe show?
faq.answer: Start from the current script, prepare a reviewed English cue list, choose and test the audience display path, then rehearse a live operator against the performance.

faq.question: Are English surtitles the same as accessibility captions?
faq.answer: Not necessarily. Surtitles translate the spoken performance; captions commonly include relevant non-speech information as well. Describe what audiences will actually receive.

faq.question: Should a Fringe show use projection or mobile surtitles?
faq.answer: Choose according to the room, audience, phone policy, network, sightlines, languages, and fallback. Projection and mobile viewing can also work together.

faq.question: Are prepared surtitles suitable for improvised work?
faq.answer: Often not as the primary service. Unscripted or frequently changing performances may need a speech-to-text reporter or a carefully tested hybrid plan.

glossary.definition: Prepared English translation displayed during a performance spoken in another language.
Audience-facing text that may include dialogue, speaker information, sound effects, music, and off-stage sound.
An ordered, editable sequence of prepared text for a live operator to trigger during performance.
A browser-based audience page opened by link or QR code, without requiring an app installation.
A rehearsed alternative for audience delivery or operator recovery if the primary display route fails.
